meta.name: Coping With the Loss of a Dog: What Grief Looks Like and What Helps
meta.title_tag: Coping With the Loss of a Dog: Grief and Guilt
meta.excerpt: Grief after losing a dog can be as intense as any other loss, and it rarely follows a neat timeline. What grief can look like, why second-guessing is so common after euthanasia, how to support children and surviving pets, and when to reach out for more help.
meta.meta_description: Losing a dog is real grief. What it can feel like, why guilt is common after euthanasia, how to help children and your other pets, and when to get support.
meta.author: Kailun Zhang

hero.alt: Empty dog bed by a window with a collar and leash resting on it

body_html:
Quick Answer: Grief after losing a dog is real grief, often as intense as losing a family member or friend (AAHA). It follows no set timeline or stages (Cornell, AVMA). Guilt is common: about half of owners question their decision after euthanasia (AAHA). Lean on people who understand, and talk to a mental health professional if sorrow or guilt hasn't eased after several weeks or disrupts daily life (Ohio State). If you're in crisis, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is free and open 24/7 in the US. When to get more help ↓

Why Losing a Dog Hurts This Much

A dog shapes every day: the walk before work, nails on the floor, a head on your knee at night. When that stops, the silence in the house can feel loud (AVMA). Part of your identity can go too. You may have been “the person who always walked the big black dog,” and AVMA counts adjusting to that as part of mourning. Research backs up what many owners feel:

  • It can be the hardest loss. In a nationally representative UK survey of 975 adults, 21.0% of those who had lost a beloved pet named it their most distressing bereavement. On a self-report questionnaire, 7.5% of people grieving a pet met criteria for prolonged grief disorder, close to the rates after losing a close friend (7.8%) or a sibling (8.9%) (Hyland, 2026). Diagnostic manuals only allow that diagnosis after a person dies.
  • Severe grief is common. About 30% of 177 Ontario clients had severe grief in the weeks after their pet died (Adams et al., 2000).

None of this is a contest. Grief can't be ranked, and yours deserves care (AVMA).

What Grief Can Look Like

Cornell's veterinary college describes grief on five levels, with no “normal” way to grieve and no prescribed timeline:

LevelWhat it can look like
PhysicalCrying, fatigue, body aches, changes in appetite or sleep, restlessness
IntellectualTrouble focusing, a sense of unreality, feeling preoccupied by the loss
EmotionalSadness, anger, guilt, anxiety, numbness, loneliness
SocialWithdrawing, wanting more or less company, feeling alone in your grief
SpiritualQuestioning beliefs, searching for meaning, wondering about an afterlife

Grief can begin before a death (Cornell). If you cared for a dog through dementia or severe arthritis, you may have been grieving for months.

It rarely follows a straight line or a set series of stages (AVMA, Cornell). It comes in waves, and many people replay their dog's last moments again and again (Ohio State). It can take a long time, sometimes up to a year, as holidays come around without your dog (Merck). If some memories blur, that doesn't mean your love is fading (Ohio State).

Guilt and the “What Ifs”

Guilt is one of the most common feelings after a pet dies (Ohio State). AVMA gives common examples: not spotting an illness sooner, not affording more treatment, choosing euthanasia too soon or too late, or an accident you feel you should have prevented. About half of owners question their decision after euthanasia (AAHA).

  • Judge the choice by what you knew then. Name your reasons at the time, before hindsight. You acted with the intention of love (Colorado State).
  • Do a reality check. A different choice could just as likely have led to the same outcome (Ohio State).
  • Remember you're human. No one is perfect, and sometimes no one is to blame (Ohio State).
  • Write it down. Some owners write an “apology letter” to their pet (Ohio State).

If the timing still weighs on you, our guides to when to euthanize a dog and the quality of life scale explain what vets look at.

When People Say “It Was Just a Dog”

Even well-meaning friends may say “it's just a dog” (AVMA). This is disenfranchised grief: a loss society doesn't fully recognize, so the support you'd expect may not come (Ohio State). Owners describe that lack of validation as a heavy part of the loss, and recognition from others as part of healing (Packman et al., 2014; Cameron, 2025).

Many people grieve privately. Among 340 US owners after euthanasia, 74.7% mourned privately, 58.2% sought social support and 0.9% joined a support group (Park & Royal, 2020).

Spend time with people who understand the loss, and set boundaries with those who don't (Cornell). Talking with others who have lost a pet can help (AVMA).

Things That Tend to Help

  • Let it be hard. Cry, and don't rush (Cornell). Talk about your memories and face the grief, rather than staying busy to avoid it (Ohio State).
  • Look after your body. Sleep and appetite often change. Walks help; if they were your dog's walks, try a different time and route at first (Ohio State).
  • Keep the bond in a new form. Look at photos, or write your dog a letter (AVMA). A review found the right “continuing bonds” can soften grief, though they can also intensify it, especially when others dismiss the loss (Hughes & Lewis Harkin, 2025). Go at your own pace.

Memorial ideas that cost little or nothing

  • A memory box with the collar, tags, a favorite toy and a paw print (Ohio State).
  • A tree or flowers planted in a spot your dog loved (AAHA, Ohio State, Cornell).
  • A photo book or journal of your dog's story: how you met, nicknames, what you'll miss most (Ohio State, Cornell).
  • A painted rock in your dog's favorite corner of the yard (Cornell).
  • A small ceremony with others who cared about your dog (Ohio State, ASPCA).
  • A donation in your dog's name to an animal charity or cause you care about, or volunteer time at a shelter or rescue (AVMA, Ohio State, Cornell).

Helping Children Grieve

For many children, a pet's death is their first real loss. Be honest: vague or inaccurate explanations can create anxiety, confusion and mistrust (AACAP).

  • Use plain words. Say “died” or “his heart stopped.” Avoid “went to sleep” or “passed away” (Ohio State). “Put to sleep” can make young children afraid to go to sleep (Ohio State, KidsHealth). If you explain euthanasia, never mention sleep alone: the vet's shot makes the dog sleep, then stops its heart (KidsHealth).
  • Match their age. Children 3 to 5 often see death as temporary; by about 9, most understand it is permanent (AACAP). Expect to repeat yourself.
  • Expect mixed feelings. Children may be angry that the dog was euthanized, or feel guilty about times they were mean to it (KidsHealth). It's okay for them to see you cry (HealthyChildren.org).
  • Tell teachers. Grief can show up at unexpected times and places, and resurface well after the death (Ohio State).
  • Let them help remember. A drawing, a collage or a planted tree can help a child say goodbye. Suggest it gently and follow their lead (AACAP, HealthyChildren.org).

Get extra help if, months later, a child still struggles with daily life at home or school, or shows deep, prolonged sadness or suicidal behavior (HealthyChildren.org). If you think your child may be thinking about suicide, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline right away (HealthyChildren.org). It's usually best not to replace the pet right away (AACAP); see getting another dog after a loss.

Your Other Dog May Grieve Too

Surviving dogs often change after a companion dies:

  • Of 159 dogs in Australia and New Zealand, 74% changed their affectionate behavior, often demanding more attention, and some sought out the lost companion's favorite spot. 35% ate less and 34% slept more (Walker et al., 2016).
  • In 426 Italian households that lost one of two dogs, only 13.4% of owners saw no change. Attention seeking rose in 67% of dogs and play dropped in 57%. About a quarter of owners (24.9%) saw changes last more than 6 months (Uccheddu et al., 2022).

In both studies, seeing the body made no difference to these changes. In the Italian study, the owner's own grief and anger predicted the dog's changes, though the authors can't confirm it was grief.

Keep routines steady, be a calm and secure base, and do things your dog enjoys; settling can take weeks to months (Cornell). Don't assume every change is grief: any change that persists needs a vet exam (Cornell). If your dog stops eating or drinking, call your vet promptly rather than waiting it out (Ohio State, Cornell). A new dog isn't a cure for a grieving one; our guide to getting another dog explains why.

When to Reach for More Help

Grief is normal, and the pain usually eases with time (Ohio State). See a trained mental health professional if sorrow or guilt hasn't eased after several weeks, or disrupts work, family or social life (Ohio State), or if depression is profound or prolonged (AVMA). ASPCA suggests talking with your doctor if severe grief persists, and your vet may be able to suggest support groups or grief counselors (AVMA).

Free pet-loss support:

  • Cornell University Pet Loss Resources and Support: a support line staffed by veterinary student volunteers who have trained with professional grief counselors. Hours vary by season, and callers can stay anonymous.
  • Tufts Pet Loss Support Helpline, at the Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine: staffed 6 to 9 p.m. Eastern, Monday through Thursday, with voicemail returned on the next shift.
  • Association for Pet Loss and Bereavement: a nonprofit whose free membership includes hosted chat rooms.
  • Humane Colorado lists a free pet loss support group that meets on Zoom on Thursday evenings.
  • ASPCA End of Life Care: guidance on euthanasia, aftercare and grief.

If you're struggling to cope: pet-loss lines are for grief, not emergencies. Cornell says its line is not a mental health hotline. If grief feels unbearable, you're thinking about ending your life, or you feel you can't go on, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in the US: free, confidential call, text and chat support, 24/7. If you're in immediate danger, contact local emergency services.

Written by Kailun Zhang, who is not a veterinarian or a counselor. This guide summarizes the veterinary, pediatric and research sources listed below and isn't a substitute for professional support.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does grief last after losing a dog?

There's no set timeline (Cornell). It can take a long time, sometimes up to a year, as holidays come around without your dog (Merck). If sorrow hasn't eased after several weeks, or disrupts daily life, consider talking to a professional (Ohio State).

Is it normal to feel guilty after putting my dog down?

Yes. About half of owners question their decision after euthanasia (AAHA). Judge it by what you knew at the time, before hindsight; you acted out of love (Colorado State).

Why does losing a dog hurt more than I expected?

Dogs are part of your daily routine and even your identity (AVMA). Grief for a pet is often as intense as for a family member or friend (AAHA), and in a UK survey, prolonged grief after losing a pet was about as common as after many human losses (Hyland, 2026).

How do I explain my dog's death to my child?

Be honest, simple and concrete. Say “died,” and avoid “put to sleep,” which can make young children afraid to go to sleep (Ohio State, KidsHealth). Young children may need it explained more than once (AACAP).

Does my other dog grieve when a companion dog dies?

Many surviving dogs seek more attention, play less or eat less, sometimes for months (Walker et al., 2016; Uccheddu et al., 2022). Keep routines steady, see your vet about any change that persists, and call promptly if your dog stops eating or drinking (Cornell, Ohio State).

When should I talk to a professional about pet grief?

If sorrow or guilt hasn't eased after several weeks or affects work, family or social life (Ohio State), or if depression is profound or prolonged (AVMA). If you have thoughts of ending your life, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988lifeline.org.
